The central distinction separates checks visible during repair search from evidence reserved for final assessment. Four worked comparative audits show how changed candidate populations, oracle rules, or execution budgets alter reported detection rates. Additional tests can expose missed faults while rejecting valid alternatives or reducing correct-repair yield under a fixed budget. Repository-level audits separate issue reproduction from candidate-patch discrimination and distinguish automated discrepancy detection from requirements-based adjudication. An evidence matrix links each coded decision to supporting passages and records shared benchmark ancestry. We specify a reporting protocol for repair benchmarks and maintenance pipelines that retains uncertain judgments and records validation cost alongside fault detection and valid-patch retention.

title: SWE-Time: Benchmarking Temporal Repository Understanding
abstract: Repository-level code-understanding benchmarks have progressively expanded the spatial scope of reasoning, from local code to entire repositories, while largely treating each repository as a static snapshot. However, how models reason about repository evolution over time remains largely unexplored. We introduce SWE-Time, a benchmark for temporal repository understanding that makes repository evolution itself the reasoning target. SWE-Time evaluates two complementary temporal directions: retrospective understanding of repository evolution through historical regression analysis and prospective understanding of intended changes from pre-change repository states. To enable realistic yet reliable evaluation in these settings, we introduce the RealWorld-to-Verifiable Construction Framework, which transforms real-world developer queries and historical evidence into verifiable evaluation tasks. We evaluate 15 coding agents on 1,661 cases from 65 GitHub repositories. Within Claude Code, Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest SWE-Time Avg. of 61.9, leaving substantial headroom. Controlled analyses highlight the importance of historical code evidence and developer intent, while consistent reasoning across repository states remains challenging. These results highlight repository evolution as a distinct and challenging dimension of code understanding.

title: Unmasking shortcut solutions of coding agents on partial differential equations
abstract: Coding agents now write simulation programs, but benchmarks usually judge only whether their output matches a reference. In manufactured-solution tasks the data determine the exact solution, so a matching output need not come from a solver. We introduce PDEViBench, a benchmark of 290 tasks in six equation families that traces each passing program to the computation behind its output and reruns unclear programs on changed data. A Codex agent (GPT-5.2) passed 80% of 1,450 runs, yet about one pass in ten returned the exact solution without solving the equation. Counting only solved passes changed which task features made problems seem hard and reversed the ranking of two prompts. Once the prompt forbade the shortcut, every pass was a numerical solve, and on tasks without a closed-form solution passing programs stayed correct on changed data. Scientific coding benchmarks should check how each answer was computed as well as whether it matches.

title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
abstract: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts
abstract: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.

title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
abstract: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

title: ControlHarbor: A Benchmark for Control Design by Coding Agents
abstract: LLM agents, i.e., language models run by a harness, can now write, run and debug software autonomously. This raises the question of whether they can also carry out control system design. In this paper, we consider control system design as a task for LLM agents and grade the designed controller as control engineers do: the controller is given in a single Python file mapping measurements to actions, evaluated on held-out seeds against an ordered set of requirements, under specified physical perturbations and structural certificates, without using neural networks. We formulate the task as a chance-constrained feasibility problem and instantiate it in ControlHarbor, a benchmark of 44 tasks over 13 plants, which includes network consensus, vehicle platooning, the MuJoCo hopper, walker and humanoid. The tasks are packaged in the Harbor format, so that any agent harness can be run against them, and the same environments also serve learning algorithms other than LLMs, such as reinforcement learning (RL), under the same evaluation. With ControlHarbor, we observe that the controllers designed by three frontier coding agents, Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1 and Sonnet 5.5, reach the RL return on every parity task, but only in a minority of sessions. We also observe that the controllers certified for return alone usually fail under perturbations. When robustness is part of the specification, a structured design meets it at the RL return on the humanoid task, where domain-randomised RL does not; under large pushes, domain-randomised RL succeeds and no designed controller does. The benchmark, the controllers, and their grades are released.

title: CoReMem: Cost-Internalizing Memory for Successive Coding Tasks with Prospective Valuation
abstract: Coding agents tackle successive tasks on an evolving repository, carrying forward edits and writing memory before the next task is known. Selecting memory for unknown next tasks requires balancing future usefulness against the costs of writing and reading it. The actor must also decide when acting on available memory saves effort as the task unfolds. We introduce Coding-Repository Memory (CoReMem), a cost-internalizing framework that guides memory design and actor adaptation through measured memory value on the next task. Prospective segment valuation compares runs of the next task with and without individual trajectory segments from the same inherited repository state, guiding a compact memory built around anchors: repository locations and executable checks. Actor adaptation estimates on-policy memory value within rollout groups with and without memory, using a reward that prioritizes resolution and penalizes step count in successful runs. Provenance-gated value credit assigns the additional value term to steps identified as using memory-supplied anchors, while every step retains outcome credit. On ChainSWE, CoReMem raises the 27B actor's resolve rate from 21.0% to 25.7%, with 17% fewer steps and 11% fewer total cache-aware tokens, including memory-module calls, relative to the untrained actor model without memory.

title: Interpreting Coding Agents Through Their Behavioral Trajectories
abstract: Standard coding-agent benchmarks primarily evaluate binary task success, treating execution as a black box and obscuring the behaviors that produce those outcomes. We analyze a large corpus of 143,209 execution trajectories from 125 agent configurations spanning 117 unique models. To enable comparisons across heterogeneous agent interfaces, we develop a rule-based parser that maps raw execution traces to high-level actions such as repository search, file editing, and test execution, and audit its predictions against a six-model consensus reference on 500 events. We find that agents with similar solve rates can nevertheless differ substantially in how they explore, modify and verify code. Moreover, without using task outcomes, token counts, or tool names as features, aggregate behavioral profiles retrieve the corresponding agent stack across disjoint repository sets and programming languages, although task composition is not fully controlled in the cross-repository setting. Through analyses of frontier models and agent scaffolds, we further show that scaffold choice and reasoning effort systematically shift agents' search, editing, and testing behavior. We release the deterministic parser together with the full annotation and analysis pipeline alongside an annotated trajectory subset.

title: SWE-CoWork: Benchmarking Coding Agents as Digital Employees in Organizations
abstract: A coding agent working within a software organization must establish what to build, collaborate with colleagues, and verify what it delivers. We introduce SWE-CoWork, a benchmark comprising 101 development assignments across 101 real repositories, 11 programming languages, and 12 application domains. Each assignment places an agent in a simulated engineering organization with 26 colleagues who have distinct responsibilities, bounded knowledge, and controlled collaboration behavior. Starting from a brief handoff, agents must recover requirements distributed across colleagues and workplace records, reconcile conflicting evidence, and implement changes evaluated by private executable tests. We evaluate eleven models and find a substantial gap between partial implementation and complete task delivery. The two leading models satisfy approximately 63% of fail-to-pass (F2P) tests but complete fewer than 8% of assignments. Providing complete requirements upfront improves F2P by approximately 16 percentage points for Seed Evolving and GPT-6 Astra, yet leaves complete task success unchanged. Requirement-level trajectory analysis reveals failures throughout the delivery process: Claude-Opus-5.5 directs a mean of 93% of first questions about queried cards to their accountable owners across runs but obtains only 64% of colleague-held requirements. Deferred questions go unfollowed, implementations remain incomplete even after requirements are acquired, and 31% of requirements reported as completed fail their tests. These findings highlight sustained requirement tracking, from clarification through implementation, verification, and handoff, as a key challenge for reliable autonomous software engineering.

title: Beyond Leaderboard Ranks: Selecting Software Engineering Agents Under Budget Constraints
abstract: Teams that adopt LLM agents for issue resolution must decide which agent to pay for, and how much to spend finding out. Leaderboard ranks give weak evidence for this decision. Accuracy differences may be statistically unresolved, reported costs may be inconsistent, and evaluating candidate agents can itself be expensive. We investigate budget-constrained agent selection using 58,197 run--task records extracted from the Holistic Agent Leaderboard (HAL), focusing on SWE-bench and six additional benchmarks. Across seven benchmarks, 27 of 35 steps along the accuracy--cost Pareto frontiers are statistically unresolved. On SWE-bench, a run costing $34.16 trails the $170.78 leader by 14.6 percentage points, but the available tasks cannot statistically distinguish their accuracy. Reported costs also differ from standardized token-based estimates by up to 11.7x, while selective task evaluation can bias estimates of full-benchmark execution cost. We therefore compare evaluation strategies under explicit evaluation budgets and deployment-cost caps. Under advance knowledge of task costs, successive halving reaches our uncertainty-aware selection target on SWE-bench using 6.6% of exhaustive evaluation spend, achieving the lowest cost on six of seven benchmarks and tying on the seventh. Its advantage narrows when task costs are unknown before execution or exact-best selection is required. Our findings motivate decision-oriented agent evaluation that accounts for accuracy uncertainty, validates execution costs, and compares complex selection methods against simple adaptive allocation.

title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
abstract: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.

title: MCP-based AI coding agent Integrating Static Analysis for Web Accessibility Error Correction
keywords: Protocols;Law;Biological system modeling;Static analysis;Encoding;Error correction codes;Servers;Artificial intelligence;Standards;Context modeling;Web accessibility;LLM;WCAG;Model Context Protocol;AI coding agents;Static Analysis
abstract: While ensuring web accessibility is becoming a legal obligation, 94.8% of the top one million websites violate WCAG standards, highlighting the need for more efficient implementation support in development environments. This paper proposes a novel approach to ensuring web accessibility using general-purpose AI coding agents by providing them with appropriate contextual information for accessibility error correction through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. This approach enables integration of Biome’s static analysis with the flexible code-base understanding capabilities of AI coding agents to efficiently produce WCAG-compliant fixes. Adopting the MCP architecture enables uniform use across various AI coding agent environments, such as Claude Code and Roo Code. We conducted experiments using an AI coding agent with four different LLM backends on a common test case and demonstrated the feasibility of our approach.

title: GHAgentFiles: A dataset of coding agent file histories in GitHub repositories
keywords: Context;Codes;Encoding;Software development management;History;Printing;Electronic mail;Tools;Evolution (biology);Software;dataset;coding agent;context file;collaborative software development;empirical software engineering
abstract: Since the introduction of coding-specific LLMs in the early 2020s, coding agents have become increasingly popular in collaborative software development projects. Since 2025, it is common practice to specify context files that provide additional context to coding agents about the project structure, development commands, coding conventions, and so on. To enable large-scale empirical studies of collaborative GitHub repositories involving coding agents, we provide a dataset of context, skill and subagent files and an open-source tool to identify and extract such files automatically. Out of an initial list of 165K+ repositories, we identify 27K+ repositories with coding agent files for six major agents (Claude, Codex, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Windsurf and Cursor), resulting in 142K+ distinct file histories and 401K+ revisions covering their evolution. We conduct a preliminary observational analysis on this large dataset and present some perspectives to the research community on how to use this dataset for future empirical studies.

title: Evolution Context Gap: An Empirical Study of Agent Manifests
keywords: Evolution (biology);Context;Law;Codes;Encoding;Modeling;Labeling;Printing;Complexity theory;Artificial intelligence;agent manifests;AI coding agents;software evolution;content analysis;CLAUDE.md;empirical study
abstract: AI coding agents—Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, and Cursor—increasingly rely on developer-authored instruction les (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, copilot-instructions.md, etc.) to understand project context. These agent manifests have not been systematically studied. We present the first large-scale content analysis of 80 real-world manifests drawn from five agent types using a six-category taxonomy and a three-model LLM classifier with majority-vote consensus. Workflow & Process dominates (present in 96.2% of manifests, 43.5% mean character fraction), while evolution context—information about how the software changes over time—is largely absent: 73.8% of manifests contain no evolution content, and none references Lehman’s laws of software evolution. A single significant project-level correlation emerges: manifests in more law-conformant projects contain more coding-style guidance (ρ = 0.431, p = 0.040, n=23). These findings characterise a systematic evolution context gap that leaves agents architecture-blind and motivate automated manifest enrichment tooling.

title: Uncovering AGENTS.md: What Testing Guidance Open Source Projects Provide to Coding Agents
keywords: Artificial intelligence;Codes;Poles and zeros;Testing;Encoding;Printing;Tools;Documentation;Software development management;Conferences;Software engineering;agentic coding;AI agents;AI guidance;software testing;open-source software
abstract: Agentic coding tools increasingly operate inside software repositories, where their behavior is shaped not only by model capabilities but also by repository context. An emerging form to provide such context is agent context files, also known as AI guidance files (e.g., AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md), which can encode project commands, conventions, and development expectations. In this paper, we study how open-source projects organize these guidance files and how they communicate testing expectations to coding agents. We analyze repositories from AIDev-pop, a collection of popular GitHub repositories with observed agent-authored pull requests. We first mine root-level AI guidance files and any Markdown files they explicitly reference to characterize repository-level organization and delegation. We find that root-level guidance is concentrated in generic AGENTS.md files and Claude-specific files, and that root guidance is not always self-contained: many repositories refer to additional resources. We then manually analyze testing guidance in a stratified sample of 300 repositories, covering 626 Markdown files and more than 3,300 coded quotations. In our sample, testing guidance is common: 249 of the 300 repositories include test commands, helping agents execute repository-specific tests. Less frequent themes on testing guidance are related to strategy, mentality, mocking, coverage, avoidance, and naming convention expectations. Overall, our results show that AI guidance files are currently mostly used to expose testing infrastructure to coding agents, but are less consistently used to make maintainer expectations about good tests explicit.

title: Execution Control Harness for Governed LLM-Based Code Generation
keywords: Modeling;Large language models;Cognition;Cognitive systems;Codes;DSL;Design methodology;Manuals;Software;Printing;LLM-based code generation;software engineering;AI-assisted development;workflow systems;domain-specific languages;software quality
abstract: LLM-based coding agents have strong potential for automating software development, but their direct application remains fragile under long and complex requirements. Specification omissions are common, and autonomous local fixes can trigger cascading regressions. In a preliminary experiment, implementing a single business function using a standard specification-driven approach required 65 interaction rounds and approximately 9 hours of manual correction.In this paper, we propose an execution control harness that tightly couples LLM-based code generation with governed execution. Implemented as a YAML-based workflow DSL, the harness integrates mechanically scoped reasoning, deterministic validation gates, automated Git-based rollback, and hybrid human-agent control.A case study on a real-world insurance application of approximately 30 KLOC suggests that the proposed approach helps suppress specification omissions and regression chains. Under comparable conditions, the number of correction iterations was reduced from 65 to 3, and total development time decreased from 9.0 to 0.5 hours. These results indicate that reliable AI-driven software development requires not only capable agents but also execution control architectures that govern the generation process.

title: Spec-Driven AI: A Multiagent Framework for Specification-Centric SDLC Automation
keywords: Context;Codes;Indexes;Indexing;Artificial intelligence;Modeling;Tools;Printing;Large language models;Evolution (biology);Spec-Driven Development;Multiagent Systems;AI-Assisted Software Engineering;Software Maintenance and Evolution;SDLC Automation
abstract: AI coding assistants are transforming software development, but most approaches remain code-centric and weakly connected to requirements, specifications, architectural decisions, organizational standards, and quality gates. This paper presents Spec-Driven AI, a multiagent framework for specification-centric Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) automation. The framework combines an SDLC orchestrator, specialized lifecycle agents, human-in-the-loop gates, auditable artifact generation, and a Pattern Manager / Context Platform that provides governed context through repository indexing, document retrieval, knowledge graph extraction, adherence validation, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools. Spec-Driven AI treats specifications as verifiable contracts and uses agents to coordinate discovery, specification, design, planning, implementation support, testing, review, and traceability. We describe the architecture, implementation, and demonstration scenario showing how a project is registered, indexed, governed, and used to prepare structured context for SDLC agents. Screencast: https://youtu.be/w4QT-nrRgNo.

title: A Knowledge Engineering Framework for AI-Driven Software Development: Harness, Guardrail, and AI-Native Knowledge DevOps
keywords: Modeling;Codes;Reviews;Artificial intelligence;Design methodology;Testing;Manuals;DevOps;Refining;Encoding;knowledge engineering;AI-driven software development;LLM coding agents;knowledge DevOps;harness engineering
abstract: Development-time knowledge—design rationale, architectural decisions, domain constraints, hard-won lessons—generated during AI-driven software development is largely ephemeral, lost between agent sessions. We propose a knowledge engineering framework whose guiding principle is pervasive AI participation—an aspirational design stance in which the agent accompanies the development workflow as broadly as practical and externalizes what it observes into machine-readable artifacts. The framework casts an Effective Agent as Foundation Model + (Harness ∥ Guardrail): two parallel operational concerns—Harness (course-setting; Knowledge, Skills, Stakeholder personas, Runtime/loader) and Guardrail (deviation detection; static analysis, automated tests, an adversarial review-gate drawing on a heterogeneous foundation-model family (untested), post-push review). A separate, external meta-process, AI-Native Knowledge DevOps (Capture/Refine/Create/Apply, GitOps-versioned, agent-loop driven), refines them across sessions: capture Guardrail findings and re-inject refined artifacts into both Harness and Guardrail. Adopting ADRs, GitOps, and concurrent harness-engineering corpora (AGENTS.md, plans, post-integration sensors, AI-rule promotion [1]–[3]) as foundations rather than novelty, our narrower contribution is a four-cell Harness, a Guardrail panel at parity, and a dual-target refinement loop (a design hypothesis we present, not an evaluated effect). A 142-day, 297-commit longitudinal experience report (a marketsizing tool for business planning under the TAM/SAM/SOM framework, built with Claude Code plus an OpenAI Codex CLI review-gate) illustrates the framework: 9,441 LOC, 441 tests, 14 knowledge documents (7,349 lines), and 92 issues (78 filed via the agent’s issue-lifecycle Skill). Commit-history analysis shows 63% of commits on the agent-loaded artifacts are maintenance-class rather than purely additive—we report this as a descriptive number, not as evidence the cycle caused the share, since the case is N=1 with the developer overlapping the framework authors.

title: Specifications as Governance Artifacts: Human–AI Collaboration and Oversight for AI-Generated Code
keywords: Codes;Modeling;Artificial intelligence;Reviews;Printing;Large language models;Contracts;Timing;Costing;Security;human-AI collaboration;AI governance;accountability in code generation;audit trails;specification-driven development;technical oversight;code generation;large language models
abstract: AI coding assistants now write a large share of production software, and they write it fast. This shifts software engineering from writing code to governing it: deciding who is accountable for AI-generated behavior, how divergence from intent is detected, and how humans and models divide the labor of oversight. Most teams lack a structured answer, and AI-generated code reaches production carrying security defects, functional bugs, and behavioral drift. We present a specification-driven governance framework that treats the specification as the primary governance artifact and the shared contract for human–AI collaboration. The framework adds a specification review gate modeled on the high-level and low-level design (HLD/LLD) reviews teams already trust; it then treats the approved specification, HLD, and LLD as an explicit, auditable baseline against which generated code is checked for drift, routing every flagged drift to a human for reconciliation. We make the collaboration concrete—defining author, reviewer, model, and reconciler roles as a responsibility assignment (RACI) and specifying the audit trail the baseline produces—and align the control points to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and the EU AI Act. We evaluate with a controlled within-subject human study of five reviewers performing baseline-anchored versus code-only drift review on real AI-generated services, and—to check robustness in a separate population—a large automated-reviewer replication (three models, 90 machine reviews) of the same design. The human study reports an honest, sharp result: an approved specification did not increase the number of drifts reviewers caught (recall 0.53 vs $0.52, \mathrm{p}=0.69$), but it made findings attributable—reviewers tied 81% of findings to a named requirement versus 0% without a baseline $(\mathrm{p}=0.043)$—and raised confidence, at a significant effort cost $(\approx 48 vs 27 min, p = 0.043)$. The automated replication produced a similar pattern. Recall remained essentially unchanged $(\mathrm{p}=0.95)$, whereas attribution increased from 0.00 to 0.67 (p < 10-4) for all models. We observed this result across reviewers rather than for only one reviewer, suggesting that the effect is associated with the review setup rather than an individual reviewer's behavior. The anonymized artifact released with the study includes the complete set of materials.

title: Methods and Techniques of Agentic Software Engineering: A Systematic Literature Review
keywords: Software engineering;Systematic literature review;Software;Codes;Software development management;Multi-agent systems;Autonomous agents;Protocols;Maintenance;Automation;Agentic software engineering;autonomous agents;multi-agent systems;code generation;software automation;systematic review
abstract: The development of agentic software engineering (ASE) is shifting the software development process, specifically by adopting autonomous agents into the fundamental software development process, where autonomous agents using large language models (LLMs) and artificial intelligence (AI) make decisions, write code, and collaborate across the entire software development lifecycle. The systematic review is a summary of literature on the agentic software engineering methodologies, frameworks, and techniques published in 2022-2025. We identify and compare methods based on autonomous coding, multi-agent systems, iterative refinement, and human-agent collaboration, drawing on 61 high-quality studies. We find that LLM-based agents show substantial potential in automated software engineering and that recent work is exploring new trends in agent cooperation, reasoning systems, and tool integration. We recognize such key challenges as the coordination procedures, reliability, explainability, and the ethical issues. This review characterizes the emerging role of agentic software engineering in improving the productivity of developers, the quality of their code, and the automation of their processes, and it offers a structured roadmap for future research. With the rapid evolution of the field, agentic approaches will tend to transform the conception, creation, and maintenance of software and provide more autonomous, adaptive, and intelligent systems.

title: Software Engineering Using Autonomous Agents: Are We There Yet?
keywords: Codes;Decision making;Transforms;Software quality;Autonomous agents;Complexity theory;Task analysis;Autonomous agents;Large Language Models (LLMs);SDLC
abstract: Autonomous agents equipped with Large Language Models (LLMs) are rapidly gaining prominence as a revolutionary technology within the realm of Software Engineering. These intelligent and autonomous systems demonstrate the capacity to perform tasks and make independent decisions, leveraging their intrinsic reasoning and decision-making abilities. This paper delves into the current state of autonomous agents, their capabilities, challenges, and opportunities in Software Engineering practices. By employing different prompts (with or without context), we conclude the advantages of contextrich prompts for autonomous agents. Prompts with context enhance user requirement understanding, avoiding irrelevant details that could hinder task comprehension and degrade model performance, particularly when dealing with complex frameworks such as Spring Boot, Django, Flask, etc. This exploration is conducted using Auto-GPT (v0.3.0), an open-source application powered by GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 which intelligently connects the “thoughts” of Large Language Models (LLMs) to independently accomplish the assigned goals or tasks.

title: Exploring Autonomous Agents: A Closer Look at Why They Fail When Completing Tasks
keywords: Bridges;Prevention and mitigation;Large language models;Taxonomy;Failure analysis;Benchmark testing;Autonomous agents;Planning;Software engineering;LLM agents;autonomous agents;failure analysis
abstract: Autonomous agent systems powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated promising capabilities in automating complex tasks. However, current evaluations largely rely on success rates without systematically analyzing the interactions, communication mechanisms, and failure causes within these systems. To bridge this gap, we present a benchmark of 34 representative programmable tasks designed to rigorously assess autonomous agents. Using this benchmark, we evaluate three popular open-source agent frameworks combined with two LLM backbones, observing a task completion rate of approximately 50%. Through in-depth failure analysis, we develop a three-tier taxonomy of failure causes aligned with task phases, highlighting planning errors, task execution issues, and incorrect response generation. Based on these insights, we propose actionable improvements to enhance agent planning and self-diagnosis capabilities. Our failure taxonomy, together with mitigation advice, provides an empirical foundation for developing more robust and effective autonomous agent systems in the future.

title: Designing Autonomous AI Agents for Code Generation, Refactoring, and Maintenance in Agile Software Engineering
keywords: Circuits;Feedback;Integrated circuits;Recommender systems;Information filtering;Circuits and systems;HTTP;Protocols;Feedback loop;Feedback communications;Autonomous AI Agents;Code Generation;Refactoring and Maintenance;Agile Software Engineering and Multi-Agent Architecture
abstract: This paper suggests a self-organizing multi-agent AI system, which would be used to automate a code generation process, refactor and software maintenance in agile development environments. The first one is the increased productivity of developers, the minimization of technical debt, and high-quality software through facilitating AI-driven, sprint-paced development processes. To do this, the study uses the Code Search Net data set as the sole data set, which implies the high-quality large consistent and high-volume training corpus of more than six million code-documentation pairs of a variety of programming languages. This is achieved by preparing the dataset to be advanced learned by preprocessing and annotating it in a strict pipeline of preprocessing and annotation that includes AST parsing, tokenizer standardization, semantic alignment and automated metadata annotation of the dataset. Methodology This paper presents a new three-agent architecture, Planner, Coder and Reviewer Agents, coupled by a common memory state and reinforced by supervised learning, reinforcement learning and behavior cloning. The system is also tested with multi-layered metrics, e.g. code quality, refactoring effectiveness, maintenance accuracy, workflow-level Agile performance indicators. It is shown that the system shows significant performance improvements compared to the leading baseline models, e.g. Codex, CodeT5, and Code BERT. The suggested framework has a BLEU score of 93.4, Refactoring Quality Score of 95.1 and a Bug-Fix Accuracy of 91.7. It also has a very low technical debt, with a Technical Debt Reduction Index of 89.6, and can execute programs more efficiently with an Execution Efficiency Gain of 41.8. These results prove the fact that the multi-agent design gives meaningful contributions to the contextual reasoning, structural code optimization, and long-term maintainability. This novelty is made through sprint conscious, autonomously communicating AI agents that recreate workflows of real developers, allowing self-enhancing, scaling, and productioncapable automation over contemporary Agile software engineering practices.

title: Agentic AI and Reinforcement Learning for Intelligent Software Development: A Systematic Review
keywords: Agentic AI;Codes;Software;Testing;Modeling;Software engineering;Tools;Maintenance engineering;Optimization;Planning;Agentic AI;Software Development;Deep Reinforcement Learning;Autonomous Agents;Code Generation;Program Repair
abstract: As software development becomes intelligent and more autonomous, Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Agentic AI are gaining interest as a means to automate complex software development tasks. The existing studies are scattered over RL-based code generation, program repair, testing, debugging, task planning, software maintenance, and autonomous AI agents, and it is hard to have a systematic understanding of their models, applications, capabilities, and research trends. This study conducts a systematic analysis of the current and available studies on RL models and Agentic AI applications in SD, based on the RL algorithms, agent architectures, software engineering tasks, datasets, evaluation metrics, and outcomes reported. It classifies conventional RL, Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) and advanced policy- and value-based approaches and investigates the planning and reasoning capabilities, as well as the use of tools, memory, feedback and multi-agent collaboration by Agentic AI in software development tasks. The results have shown that the use of RL and Agentic AI can enhance the quality of code generation, automated testing, defect detection, program repair, task planning, and increase efficiency in the development process, and that agentic architectures offer more autonomy and adaptability than traditional approaches to code generation and automation. However, issues of design of rewards, computational costs, reliability, control of hallucinations, standardized benchmarks, security and reproducibility are yet to be addressed. This systematic study offers a unified research viewpoint and future research opportunities for creating reliable, explainable, secure, and autonomous software engineering systems using AI.

title: Transforming Software Development: A Study on the Integration of Multi-Agent Systems and Large Language Models for Automatic Code Generation
keywords: Productivity;Technological innovation;Codes;Large language models;Collective intelligence;Software;Standards;Software development management;Software engineering;Multi-agent systems;Multi-Agent;Generative AI;LLM;Software Development
abstract: This paper explores the integration of Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) and Large Language Models (LLMs) for auto-matic code generation, addressing the limitations of traditional manual coding. By conducting a comprehensive review of existing literature and analyzing a practical case study, we demonstrate how MAS and LLMs can collaboratively enhance software development processes. The research focuses on the technical and theoretical challenges of this integration, highlighting the potential for improved productivity, adaptability, and quality in code generation. The findings contribute to AI-based software engineering by revealing new research directions in collective intelligence and automated programming.

title: Complexity Backpressure for AI Coding Agents: A Cross-Model Study on Substantive Software Tasks
keywords: Complexity theory;Modeling;Codes;Artificial intelligence;Testing;Measurement;Printing;Tools;Encoding;Feedback;code complexity;maintainability;AI coding agents;SWE-bench;complexity backpressure;software engineering
abstract: AI coding agents can solve a large fraction of real-world software engineering tasks, yet the complexity and maintainability of their patches remain poorly understood and largely uncontrolled. We present Wily v2, a high-performance code-analysis tool that computes code complexity at over 570000 LOC/s, and integrate it as a complexity backpressure signal inside an agentic coding harness. To evaluate Wily on substantive tasks, we construct SWE-bench Complex, a dataset of 116 real GitHub issues from major Python projects with a median patch size of 48 lines (6.9× SWE-bench Verified). We evaluated three frontier models under control and Wily-feedback conditions. A single round of Wily feedback significantly reduces cyclomatic complexity by 20–31% and cognitive complexity by 39–54% across all three models.

title: From LLM Reasoning to Autonomous AI Agents: A Comprehensive Review
keywords: Modeling;Large language models;Cognition;Cognitive systems;Artificial intelligence;Tools;Codes;Design methodology;Retrieval augmented generation;Protocols;Autonomous AI agents;agentic AI;benchmarks;large language models;reasoning
abstract: Large language models and autonomous AI agents have evolved rapidly, resulting in a diverse array of evaluation benchmarks, frameworks, and collaboration protocols. Driven by the growing need for standardized evaluation and integration, we systematically consolidate these fragmented efforts into a unified framework. However, the landscape remains fragmented and lacks a unified taxonomy or comprehensive survey. Therefore, we present a side-by-side comparison of benchmarks developed between 2019 and 2025 that evaluate these models and agents across multiple domains. In addition, we propose a taxonomy of approximately 60 benchmarks that cover general and academic knowledge reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, code generation and software engineering, factual grounding and retrieval, domain-specific evaluations, multimodal and embodied tasks, task orchestration, and interactive assessments. Furthermore, we review AI-agent frameworks introduced between 2023 and 2025 that integrate large language models with modular toolkits to enable autonomous decision-making and multi-step reasoning. Moreover, we present real-world applications of autonomous AI agents in materials science, biomedical research, academic ideation, software engineering, synthetic data generation, chemical reasoning, mathematical problem-solving, geographic information systems, multimedia, healthcare, and finance. We then survey key agent-to-agent collaboration protocols, namely the Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A). Finally, we discuss recommendations for future research, focusing on advanced reasoning strategies, failure modes in multi-agent LLM systems, automated scientific discovery, dynamic tool integration via reinforcement learning, integrated search capabilities, and security vulnerabilities in agent protocols.

title: Leveraging Agentic Coding for Interactive Education in Electrical Engineering
keywords: Codes;Printing;Equations;Large language models;Modeling;Aluminum;Context;Displays;Modules (abstract algebra);Simulation;Agentic coding;LLM agents;virtual laboratories;electrical engineering education;authoring workflow;transient analysis;eddy currents;numerical methods
abstract: Large language models enable the automated synthesis of interactive educational software beyond conversational tutoring. This paper presents an authoring methodology using agentic coding (an autonomous, tool-augmented workflow based on the Reason-and-Act (ReAct) paradigm) to generate standalone, browser-based simulation modules for electrical engineering curricula. It was applied across three undergraduate courses, using three distinct agentic development environments: a transient commutation simulator for second-order RLC circuits (circuit theory), an eddy-current induction laboratory (electromagnetism), and an interactive benchmark of iterative linear solvers (numerical methods). We formalize a pipeline built on (1) strict decoupling of pedagogical specification from implementation, (2) formal mathematical notation constraints, (3) singlepass holistic generation to prevent context window degradation, (4) human-in-the-loop validation gates, and (5) prompt-level regeneration rather than conversational code patching. Recurring failure modes: notation drift, context saturation, feature creep, and physically invalid simulations ("vibe physics"); are analyzed together with their mitigations, and an independent analytical audit of two generated modules is reported. Modules are synthesized in 5–10 minutes over 3–5 specification iterations, shifting instructor effort from manual programming to requirements engineering and domain verification.

title: Human-Machine Teaming and Team Effectiveness in AI Tools for Software Engineering
keywords: Analytical models;Human-machine systems;Object recognition;Artificial intelligence;Monitoring;Software engineering;Lenses
abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support software engineering (SE), shifting the role of AI tools for SE (AI4SE) towards team members rather than simply tools. Human-machine teaming (HMT) views humans and machines as members of a team. This approach may be useful in AI4SE but HMT and team effectiveness have received little attention in the software engineering community. Objective: To unpick whether and how HMT and team effectiveness have been applied in AI4SE, and to identify recommendations. Method: A mapping study approach identifies 21 papers on developercentred AI4SE. Each one is analysed to identify its use of HMT, its focus regarding AI-developer interaction, and any elements of team effectiveness. Results: Different aspects of AI-developer interaction have been considered but only one paper explicitly uses the HMT concept. Some elements of team effectiveness are considered, but others are not addressed at all, and several studies do not consider any. Conclusion: Researchers are encouraged to consider HMT as a framework for AI4SE, to leverage research in all-human teams, adaptive UX and developer motivation to inform tool design, and reduce reliance on human monitoring.

title: Coding Agents in the Wild: Failure Modes and Rejection Patterns of AI-Generated Pull Requests
keywords: Codes;Reviews;Labeling;Encoding;Modeling;Testing;Artificial intelligence;Large language models;Taxonomy;Design methodology;Agentic workflows;coding agents;large language models (LLMs);pull requests;software engineering;socio-technical systems
abstract: Autonomous coding agents increasingly submit pull requests (PRs) to real software repositories, making it important to evaluate their behavior under actual review, testing, and governance workflows rather than only through synthetic benchmarks. This paper investigates how agent-generated pull request (APR) rejection evolves over time, which visible failure modes are most evident among commented rejected APRs (RAPRs), and how these findings inform more effective coding-agent deployment and design. We follow a three-phase methodology. First, we construct an APR cohort from the AIDev-POP subset of the AIDev dataset, covering 12,433 APRs from 1,495 popular repositories and five coding agents. Second, we develop a socio-technical taxonomy of rejection reasons and validate a large language model (LLM)-based classifier on a manually labeled ground-truth subset of commented RAPRs, achieving 85.5% accuracy in identifying the main bucket reasons of the rejection. Third, we model temporal rejection patterns and conduct stratified analyses across agents, deployment settings, and reviewer types. Observational results show a significant decline in APR rejection odds over time after accounting for differences in change size, documentation and test updates, and agent type. This decline is not limited to a single agent in particular. Empirical results show that documentation co-changes are associated with lower rejection odds, whereas test-touch and patch size provide weaker differentiation. Most RAPRs are silent, with 84.2% closed without inline reviewer feedback. Among commented RAPRs, functional failures are the dominant visible rejection pattern, especially specification mismatch and logic defects. Overall, APR outcomes reflect interactions among agent behavior, repository guardrails, and developer practices. We translate these findings into evidence-informed design principles and advocate reflexive coding agent as a new design pattern that emphasizes context acquisition, local validation, and closer alignment with repository expectations. Our replication package is available at: https://github.com/mahdhindi/coding-agents-wild

title: RepoTransBench: A Real-World Multilingual Benchmark for Repository-Level Code Translation
keywords: Translation;Codes;Benchmark testing;Multilingual;Source coding;Manuals;Large language models;Python;Neural networks;Complexity theory;Repository-level code translation;multilingual benchmark;LLM-based agent
abstract: Repository-level code translation refers to translating an entire code repository from one programming language to another while preserving the functionality of the source repository. Many benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate the performance of such code translators. However, previous benchmarks mostly provide fine-grained samples, focusing at either code snippet, function, or file-level code translation. Such benchmarks do not accurately reflect real-world demands, where entire repositories often need to be translated, involving longer code length and more complex functionalities. To address this gap, we propose a new benchmark, named RepoTransBench, which is a real-world multilingual repository-level code translation benchmark featuring 1,897 real-world repository samples across 13 language pairs with automatically executable test suites. Besides, we introduce RepoTransAgent, a general agent framework to perform repository-level code translation. We evaluate both our benchmark’s challenges and agent’s effectiveness using several methods and backbone LLMs, revealing that repository-level translation remains challenging, where the best-performing method achieves only a 32.8% success rate. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that translation difficulty varies significantly by language pair direction, with dynamic-to-static language translation being much more challenging than the reverse direction (achieving below 10% vs. static-to-dynamic at 45-63%). Finally, we conduct a detailed error analysis and highlight current LLMs’ deficiencies in repository-level code translation, which could provide a reference for further improvements. We provide the code and data at https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/RepoTransBench.

title: Can AI Agents Generate Microservices? How Far are We?
keywords: Codes;Modeling;Printing;Testing;Artificial intelligence;Complexity theory;Costing;Costs;Application programming interfaces;Large language models;Software Architecture;Microservices;AI agents
abstract: Context. LLMs have advanced code generation, but their use for generating microservices with explicit dependencies and API contracts remains understudied.Goal. We examine whether AI agents can generate functional microservices and how different forms of contextual information influence their performance.Method. We assess 144 generated microservices across 3 agents, 4 projects, 2 prompting strategies, and 2 scenarios. Incremental generation operates within existing systems and is evaluated with unit tests. Clean state generation starts from requirements alone and is evaluated with integration tests. We analyze functional correctness, code quality, and efficiency.Results. Minimal prompts outperformed detailed ones in incremental generation, with 50–76% unit test pass rates. Clean state generation produced higher integration test pass rates (81–98%), indicating strong API contract adherence. Generated code showed lower complexity than human baselines. Generation times varied widely across agents, averaging 6–16 minutes per service.Conclusions. AI agents can produce microservices with maintainable code, yet inconsistent correctness and reliance on human oversight show that fully autonomous microservice generation is not yet achievable.

title: Evaluating LLM Coding Agents on SZ-Family Lossy Compression Across Architectures
keywords: Modeling;Codes;Optimization;Information rates;Large language models;Throughput;Architecture;Computer architecture;Graphics processing units;Printing;LLM coding agents;lossy compression;HPC;CUDA;Cerebras;evaluation benchmark
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents are increasingly applied to code translation and optimization, yet their effectiveness in performance-critical high-performance computing (HPC) settings remains poorly characterized. This paper evaluates LLM-based coding workflows on SZ-family error-bounded lossy compression kernels, which combine numerical constraints with memory-intensive and control-flow-heavy implementations. We study two representative CUDA workloads (SZp and SZx) and target two heterogeneous execution platforms: NVIDIA GPUs and Cerebras wafer-scale accelerators. Focusing on single-agent iterative generation, we analyze not only final throughput but also agent runtime behavior, including iteration patterns, sensitivity to prompt specification, and characteristic failure modes. Our results reveal a pronounced cross-architecture divergence. On GPUs, stronger models can achieve substantially higher throughput but exhibit increased sensitivity to prompt precision and optimization guidance, whereas on Cerebras the dominant challenge lies in producing runnable programs under a PE-centric spatial execution model. We further observe that LLM agents are more effective on modular kernels (SZx) than on tightly coupled bit-level pipelines (SZp), where structural dependencies hinder optimization progress. These findings suggest that evaluating LLM coding agents for HPC requires accounting for both performance outcomes and architecture-specific robustness, and that success on thread-based platforms does not directly transfer to spatial accelerators.

title: Coding Agents: A Comprehensive Survey of Automated Bug Fixing Systems and Benchmarks
keywords: Surveys;Large language models;Scalability;Semantics;Debugging;Maintenance engineering;Benchmark testing;Software;Software engineering;Context modeling;Agent-Based Models;Automated Program Repair;Large Language Models;Multi-Agent Systems;Context-Aware Debugging;Software Engineering Automation;Debugging Benchmarks;AI in Software Development
abstract: One of the trickiest problems in software engineering is automating software issue fixes, which calls for a thorough comprehension of contextual relationships, code semantics, and dynamic debugging techniques. The development of automatic program repair (APR) is examined in this survey, which traces a path from early template and constraint-based approaches to more recent developments powered by large language models (LLMs). Three main paradigms are compared here: retrieval-augmented approaches that integrate external knowledge sources, agent-based systems that use multi-agent frameworks, and agentless systems that use simplified repair pipelines. Real-world benchmarks that mimic actual engineering workflows and repository-level difficulties, such as SWE-bench, CODEAGENT-BENCH, and CodeRAG-Bench, are used to assess these cutting-edge technologies. This study demonstrates how agentic, agentless, and retrieval-augmented systems use LLMs to achieve previously unheard-of precision and scalability by following the shift from localized, single-file solutions to solving complicated, multi-file, and repository-wide difficulties. According to our findings, while complex agent architectures have potential, straightforward test-time scaling frequently produces better outcomes, especially when paired with containerized environments that allow for parallel exploration. Additionally, the survey looks at industrial applications, emphasizing effective connections with quality assurance and DevOps procedures. In order to further the development of more resilient and flexible APR frameworks that blend in perfectly with contemporary software engineering practices, we conclude by highlighting important issues in context handling and validation and suggesting future research directions in improved contextual models, human-AI collaboration, and multi-modal debugging systems.

title: Towards an Evaluation Methodology for AI Code Assistants
keywords: Artificial intelligence;Modeling;Tools;Context;Codes;Measurement;Indexes;Indexing;Printing;Manuals;Generative AI;Code Assistants;Developer Experience;Evaluation Methodology;AI-Native IDE
abstract: The integration of Generative AI into software development has introduced a paradigm shift from manual coding to AI-assisted orchestration. While numerous AI code assistants exist, there is still a lack of comprehensive methodologies to evaluate their real-world efficacy. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on code generation correctness, often neglecting the holistic Developer Experience (DX), interaction friction, and the cognitive load required to manage project context. In this paper, we propose AI-DevEval, a concrete, multi-dimensional evaluation methodology. We establish specific requirements and metrics across four axes: Efficiency & Flow, Feature Richness, Context Engineering, and User Experience. Furthermore, we apply this methodology in a controlled study with developers of varying seniority to evaluate and compare current AI code assistants across three distinct tiers: a web-based chatbot, an IDE plugin, and an AI-native IDE. Our results demonstrate that autonomous global context management and tight IDE integration significantly reduce developer friction, highlighting that the software orchestration layer is becoming as critical as the underlying language model itself.

title: Symbio Coding: An Educational Testbed for AI Agent Simulation as Software Development Team Member
keywords: Productivity;Education;Project management;Focusing;Agile software development;Encoding;Artificial intelligence;Software development management;AI agents;software development;Agile and Waterfall;simulation;AnyLogic
abstract: This paper presents an educational simulation model for integrating AI agents into software development teams. The model is proposed for use by master's students in IT project management courses to study the effectiveness of this type of AI application, which the authors call “symbio coding”. By reviewing the existing literature, we identify a research gap in understanding the practical implementation and impact of AI agents in traditional and agile software development methodologies. We propose a simulation model of an organizational structure for integrating AI into the software development process (Waterfall and Agile), describing potential roles, benefits, and challenges. Finally, we propose a simulation experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, focusing on assessing the reduction in development time due to the use of AI agents.

title: SE-Blackboard: A Shared-State Architecture for Multi-Agent Software Engineering Pipelines
keywords: Architecture;Computer architecture;Modeling;Pipelines;Software engineering;Large language models;Codes;Tools;Multi-agent systems;Testing;Multi-agent systems;large language models;software engineering;blackboard architecture;shared state;communication architecture;information fidelity;SWE-bench
abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly used for software engineering tasks, yet the role of communication architecture in these systems remains poorly understood. Most existing approaches assume message passing, where agents exchange sequential natural-language summaries, without examining the information loss this assumption may introduce. This paper makes a methodological and diagnostic contribution to that question. We present SE-Blackboard, a modular framework that places message passing, a shared-state blackboard, and a hybrid design within an otherwise identical multi-agent pipeline, and we introduce the Information Fidelity Score (IFS), a stage-level metric that measures how well key technical entities from the original issue survive successive agent handoffs. On 50 SWE-bench Lite issues, the blackboard configuration improves Coder-stage IFS by 62% over message passing (0.586 vs. 0.362) and correct file targeting by 27.5 percentage points (82.6% vs. 55.1%). Once the correct file is identified, however, all configurations converge to a ~22% conditional resolve rate, revealing a downstream bottleneck in LLM diff generation. Building on these decompositions, we present an information-flow bottleneck model that predicts how upstream gains attenuate at the patch-generation stage; the model accounts for the modest end-to-end resolve-rate improvement observed (16% vs. 12%). These findings identify communication architecture as a measurable, separable design dimension and supply tools—IFS and the bottleneck model—for diagnosing where future improvements in multi-agent SE pipelines should be targeted.

title: Exploring the Relationship Between Code Metrics and the Ability of Large Language Models to Solve Code Issues
keywords: Correlation coefficient;Codes;Correlation;Large language models;Market research;Complexity theory;Indexes;Software measurement;Software engineering;Software development management
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into software engineering workflows, assisting with tasks such as code generation, unit testing, and bug resolution. Despite their growing use, limited research has examined how code-level metrics such as Halstead complexity, maintainability index, and source lines of code correlate with issue resolution rates for LLM-powered agents when modifying existing codebases. The paper bridges the well established field of code metrics with the emerging domain of AI software engineering agents by exploring correlations between these metrics and the success of LLM driven agents in resolving GitHub issues. The key contribution is a quantitative analysis of the relationship between code metrics and LLM agent issue resolution success. Preliminary results show varying degrees of biserial correlation across models, with coefficients reaching $\mathbf{0. 4}$ for maintainability index and issue resolution. These findings suggest that code metrics can inform the evaluation of LLM coding agents and offer insights into improving models and finding indicators of issue resolution success. This research underscores the importance of maintainable, high-quality code not only for human developers but also for LLM-driven agents. Our hypothesis is that LLMs can generate correct patches or semi-automated fixes more successfully when the underlying codebase already exhibits strong maintainability and code quality metrics. Furthermore, as LLM-generated code becomes part of long-lived software products-reviewed, integrated, and extended by both humans and potentially future LLM agents-its maintainability and quality remain critical.

title: DriftBench: Detecting LLM Coding Agent Cheating via Specification-Level Constraint Drift Mutation
keywords: Modeling;Testing;Codes;Signal detection;Equations;Conferences;Detectors;Timing;Aluminum;Security;Large Language Model;Reward hacking;Specification-level mutation;Code generation testing;AI safety benchmark
abstract: For the cheating behaviour of LLM coding intelligences exploiting test case vulnerabilities, the existing test value mutation-based detection methods cannot cover the scenarios in which the intelligences exploit specification-level hidden constraints for cheating, and there is a structural detection blind spot. In this paper, we propose DriftBench with a new Drift mutation strategy, i.e., constructing the third class of impossible tasks by injecting hidden constraints into the function specification without modifying any test assertions, and designing a lightweight cheating detector based on 25-dimensional feature fusion. On 95 coding tasks constructed with reference to the IMPOSSIBLEBENCH benchmark design methodology, 1900 experimental runs were conducted using 5 models (covering the 3 model families DeepSeek, Qwen, and Zhipu). The results show that the baseline pass rate BPR is 90.3%, the One-Off cheating rate is 53.9%, the Drift cheating rate is 90.3%, the complementary detection rate DCR is 39.5%, and Drift independently detects 33 One-Off missed cheating cases; the Conflicting mutation cheating rate is only 4.4%, which is close to the absolute defence, verifying that contradiction assertion injection as an effective defence strategy. Ablation experiments further reveal that Drift cheating is insensitive to prompt wording, while One-Off cheating rate doubles from 15% to 30% with loose cues, indicating that specification-level cheating cannot be mitigated by cue word engineering.5 models show consistent cheating behaviour, validating the cross-model robustness found by DriftBench.

title: Design-First Governance for Reliable AI-Assisted Software Development
keywords: Modeling;Artificial intelligence;Codes;Design methodology;Contracts;Printing;Tools;Context;Application programming interfaces;Architecture;Software Architecture;AI-Assisted Development;Design-First;Architectural Governance;Code Generation;Large Language Models
abstract: AI coding agents operate tactically rather than strategically. While highly productive in isolated tasks, their limited context windows and behavioral unpredictability lead to technical debt accumulation and gradual architectural degradation. Consequently, large-scale production systems become increasingly difficult to maintain. We argue that reliable AI-assisted development requires establishing architectural gravity: structural constraints that guide and stabilize agent behavior over time. We demonstrate this through a Design-First workflow that instruments a contract-driven development environment for fullstack systems. Domain models are transformed into productionready backend APIs aligned with established patterns, while simultaneously generating constraint layers that embed system intent, reduce architectural drift, and preserve long-term maintainability. We evaluated this across system bootstrapping and complex feature extensions using both proprietary and open-weight LLMs. The results demonstrate that embedding architectural intent into workflow constraints enforces design goals automatically and preserves long-term maintainability. Notably, open-weight models achieved comparable architectural compliance to proprietary models under governance, indicating that well-structured constraints reduce dependence on frontier model capabilities. These findings suggest that reliable AI-assisted development is fundamentally an architectural governance challenge rather than a model capability problem.

title: Vibe Coding: A New Paradigm in Software Development Assisted by Artificial Intelligence
keywords: Codes;Encoding;Artificial intelligence;Modeling;Security;Timing;Testing;Software;Authentication;Logic;vibe coding;artificial intelligence;software development;Large Language Models;software security;Claude;Visual Studio Code;productivity
abstract: Vibe coding is an emerging approach in which developers and non-technical users describe desired functionalities in natural language, delegating actual code generation to an artificial intelligence model. This paper presents a structured case study of vibe coding through a practical experiment, using Visual Studio Code and Anthropic's Claude model to build a functional web application. We document how the vibe coding workflow operates in practice, compare the estimated development time against a conventional manual implementation of the same application, and examine the security posture of the resulting software through a structured audit. While the artificial intelligence (AI) assisted process demonstrated a notable reduction in implementation time - illustrative of a single-user, single-application scenario and not generalizable beyond it - the security audit identified several categories of vulnerabilities in the generated codebase, suggesting that vibe coding may not reliably produce secure software in this case study. The study further identifies inherent risks of this paradigm, including potential exposure of sensitive data and the difficulty of auditing automatically generated code. We also propose a conceptual clarification between vibe coding and agentic coding paradigms. We conclude that vibe coding democratizes access to software development but requires rigorous oversight frameworks to be adopted responsibly.

title: How AI Agents Are Transforming Software Engineering and the Future of Product Development
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents are revolutionizing software engineering, boosting productivity while creating new demands for skilled engineers and raising critical ethical challenges.

title: Observatory software management in the era of AI-assisted software engineering
keywords: AI-assisted Software Engineering;Agentic Coding;Software Management;Spec-Driven Development;Observatory Control Software;Coding Agents;Software Governance;Large Language Models
abstract: Thanks to advancements in generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), the last 5 years have seen exponential growth in the adoption of AI-Assisted software engineering across many industries.
